lines.text: Bar culture in Britain encompasses far more than drinking — it is a social institution woven into the fabric of daily life. The pub (public house) remains the cornerstone: a communal space for after-work pints, Sunday lunches, quiz nights, and community gatherings. 'Your local' — the pub nearest your home — holds a special place in British identity. Ordering at the bar (not table service, traditionally) follows unwritten rules: you wait your turn, the bartender acknowledges you with a nod, and you pay per round. The 'round system' — where each person takes turns buying drinks for the entire group — is a deeply embedded social ritual. Skipping your round is a serious social faux pas. Wine bars emerged in the 1980s as a more sophisticated alternative — catering to a growing interest in wine beyond pub plonk. Cocktail bars followed in the 2000s, bringing craft mixology to British cities. The gastropub — a pub serving restaurant-quality food — blurred the line between drinking and dining. Today's bar landscape includes rooftop bars, hotel bars, craft beer taprooms, natural wine bars, and alcohol-free bars. Licensing laws have evolved: historically, pubs closed at 11pm sharp (the origin of 'last orders'); the 2003 Licensing Act enabled flexible hours, though most still close between midnight and 2am. The rise of 'sober curious' culture means bars now cater to non-drinkers with equal care — quality mocktails, alcohol-free beers, and inclusive menus.

lines.text: The Decline and Revival of Pubs
lines.name: The Decline and Revival of Pubs

lines.text: Britain has lost thousands of pubs since the 2000s — rising costs, cheap supermarket alcohol, and changing habits. However, community campaigns to save 'locals', the gastropub movement, and craft beer culture have revived many. Pubs listed as 'Assets of Community Value' receive legal protection.
lines.name: Britain has lost thousands of pubs since the 2000s — rising costs, cheap supermarket alcohol, and changing habits. However, community campaigns to save 'locals', the gastropub movement, and craft beer culture have revived many. Pubs listed as 'Assets of Community Value' receive legal protection.

lines.text: Britain's first fully alcohol-free bars opened in the 2020s — serving zero-proof spirits, mocktails, and alcohol-free beers in a bar atmosphere. They reflect the growing 'sober curious' movement, particularly among younger adults who want the social experience without the alcohol.
